en: The *Kāśyapa-saṃgīti Sūtra*, translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han:
Thus have I heard. At one time, not long after the World-Honored One had entered parinirvāṇa, all the Arhats assembled.
They deliberated together;
regarding the various discussions on the collection of the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma that had not yet been finalized,
each thought to himself:
We have accomplished what was to be done;
we have crossed the mountain of afflictions and dried up the river of craving.
O Buddha, the Sun of All-Knowledge!
The divine eye among the gods suddenly vanished.
We were weary and disgusted with bearing this body;
now, desiring parinirvāṇa, he spoke these verses:
Having crossed the abyss of the foolish, the ocean of affection so difficult to traverse,
and having shattered the decay of worldly existence and the wheel of birth and death,
he beholds all manner of beings attached to their bodies as if they were baskets containing venomous snakes.
"We shall enter parinirvāṇa," thought these countless thousands of arhats, each according to his own inclinations;
their minds were as pure as an extinguished lamp.
Amidst the deep banks of a mountain cliff where rivers and springs flow,
he entered parinirvāṇa there, exhausting all his attachments and cravings,
like a lamp suddenly extinguished.
At that time, the countless thousands of arhats and others all entered parinirvāṇa.
Mahākāśyapa remained in the sky above, saying:
"Now these true persons have attained peace through extinction."
Thereupon, the deva spoke in verse:
Proclaiming the noble sound, His mind has long been unimpeded;
Now he has passed away— The Buddha is the one who extinguishes defilement and brings peace.
"Like a leader who should guide the multitude, you have attained concentration and abandoned wisdom;
suddenly, the profound darkness of delusion has appeared, and the light of the Dharma’s virtues is no longer seen.
When the Venerable Kāśyapa heard these words, he [reflected].
He thought to himself:
"How wonderful are the words of the Deva!
Before long, this world shall once again fall into profound darkness."
"What should be done about this?
He thought to himself and immediately understood:
"Now, to summarize the essential meaning, I shall compile the Sūtras and the Vinaya."
The transformation of all dharmas is for the purpose of employing compassion to bring peace and security to the world. Why is this?
Because the World-Honored One has practiced his conduct throughout incalculable eons.
Having accumulated merit and cultivated virtue through immeasurable hardship and toil,
he sought to bring peace to the world by gathering this Dharma and Vinaya to rescue and sustain it. Thus,
he upheld and protected the Buddha-dharma until all those who were to be transformed had attained parinirvāṇa.
"We should now gather together to protect and uphold the Dharma and its transformation. Thereupon,
the Venerable Mahākāśyapa and others addressed the assembly of bhikṣus, saying:
Anuruddha and the other disciples of the Muni have perished;
the adamantine mountain of impermanence has collapsed,
and the Buddha, the supreme sun, has set.
It is an extraordinary darkness and obscuration;
the light of the Muni is an extraordinary sun that dries up the ocean of the Buddhas,
and it is an extraordinary fire that consumes all-encompassing wisdom.
Now is precisely the time.
Constantly protect the world by recollecting your father's merit;
you should establish your father’s legacy and honor your father’s teachings.
To ensure that what has been done is brought to completion, it is said in verse:
Before the unsurpassed meaning is finalized, One should not abandon the attainment of nirvāṇa;
Providing full security for the sons of the Buddha, One must collect the various sūtra scrolls.
Thereupon, as soon as the assembly of bhikṣus had finished speaking thus,
the Venerable Kāśyapa and five hundred arhats desired to compile and correctly codify the meaning of the Dharma and Vinaya.
He then proceeded to Rājagṛha for the assembly of the annual *pravāraṇā*.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was also completing his year of seniority.
The elder monks thought to themselves as follows:
This Ānanda is the younger brother of the World-Honored One;
furthermore, having constantly attended upon him in person and heard his teachings,
he maintains great wisdom and understands all dharmas.
At that time, the noble assembly exclaimed in praise:
"In this harmonious multitude, they revere the Buddha's teachings as one holds a fruit in the palm of the hand;
they are praised by the One of Ten Powers, and their speech consists of pure upholding and wisdom."
Thereupon, on the fifteenth day of the seventh month,
when the new year had concluded,
they gathered together the various collections of the sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Abhidharma.
Five hundred arhats were all assembled together.
The elder Mahākāśyapa addressed the venerable Aniruddha:
"Venerable sir, observe the world: who is it that is devoid of the ten powers?"
"Among the assembly of the Tathāgata’s disciples,
which Arhat has completed what was to be done and yet does not come to this gathering?
Thereupon, Aniruddha immediately surveyed the world with his divine eye.
He replied, "Venerable Mahākāśyapa,
there is an elder named Kakuṇḍopadhāna."
While he was celebrating the New Year in the Śrī-deva palace, he did not come to the assembly;
only Mahākāśyapa should dispatch a messenger of the Sangha to invite him here.
At that time, there was among the assembly a junior member,
a bhikṣu who had newly received the full precepts three years prior;
the bhikṣu’s name was Puṇṇa.
Having severed the three impurities, he attained the three types of supernormal knowledge;
having mastered the Tripiṭaka, he acquired the three insights.
Unattached to the triple world, he attained sovereign mastery.
Thereupon, Mahākāśyapa addressed the assembly of monks,
saying, "Young bhikṣu, son, can you act as a messenger for the community of monks?
At that time, the venerable Punna rose from his seat and stood with palms joined.
"I shall receive your venerable instruction and immediately put it into practice. Mahākāśyapa said,
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Monks, it is most excellent that there is such a young bhikṣu among the noble assembly of the holy ones.
Having said this, he spoke in verse:
Śrī, with its various kinds of flowers, radiant and flourishing;
go quickly to that place where the bridge-like bowl of the Ṛṣis dwells, possessing superior supernatural powers. Just as bees gather soft fragrances, so too does he abide in excellence.
Having properly received the instructions of the assembly, I proclaim this intent for the sake of transformation:
"Mahākāśyapa and the rest of the Saṃgha have sent me to inform you of this undertaking for the flourishing of the Saṃgha; come quickly by the appointed time."
Thereupon, the worthy Ananda,
having received this command from the assembly of arhats,
leaped forth like a golden-winged garuḍa from the palace of the nāgas.
In the time it takes for a person to blink an eye, he arrived at the place of Kevaddha.
He prostrated himself at his feet, conversed with him, and after exchanging greetings, spoke this verse:
Tranquil and excellent by nature, delighting in concentration, cessation, and discipline,
with a pure mind— Kāśyapa is pure. Together with other honored ones, the Sovereigns,
and the assembled community of monks, the Buddha most excellently manifests the immeasurable.
Driven by desire for life’s necessities, he descended and saw the assembly’s excellence.
Thereupon, the worthy Kātyāyanīputra, hearing Unnābha’s words,
reflected in his mind for a moment and said to Unnābha:
O Benevolent One, it is not so.
There are monks who have attained freedom from strife, discord, contention, and litigation;
this is the teaching of the Wheel of Dharma turned by the One of Ten Powers.
Are you not disturbed by the various heterodox paths?
Are those of external ways and the beasts, like startled deer,
not seeking to destroy the Buddha-dharma through their desires?
Could it be that you wish to obstruct the brilliance of the sun with the light of a firefly?
Could it be that you, while not possessing a tranquil mind, merely assume the appearance of a śramaṇa;
lacking the conduct of a brahmacārin, yet claiming for yourself purity?
Furthermore, O Venerable One, you should not speak thus.
The Buddha told the assembly of bhikṣus: "I have taught and instructed you, yet you, on the contrary, claim that the assembly of bhikṣus such as Kāśyapa lacks great compassion."
The World-Honored One is about to enter parinirvāṇa; will there not be those who misrepresent wisdom?
The world’s treasures will no longer be seen, and heterodox paths will disturb and disorder the teachings of the True Dharma.
If there were no King who turns the Wheel of Dharma, possessed of the ten powers, sovereign, and eternal,
and if he were suddenly not seen, would it not mean the absence of great compassion?
[He is the one] who brings peace and security to all and protects all sentient beings.
Is it not so that while remaining in quiescence, the Buddha-sun does not set?
Is it not as when the Buddha is likened to moonlight— attaining freedom from obstruction and being without concealment—
and when the excellence of the blossoming flowers of the awakening-mind arises at the Tree of the Path?
The fruits of the śramaṇa’s life are subject to impermanence.
Will not the great lamp of the world be extinguished by the wind of impermanence?
Will not the fire of the Buddha be quenched by the waters of impermanence?
If there were no foolish sons to dispute and disturb the Buddha’s teachings,
the Wheel of Dharma would not have been turned back and withdrawn;
the radiant light of the Buddha-moon would not have come to an end.
The asuras obstructed the great radiance.
At that time, the worthy Pūrṇa said:
"O Kauṇḍinya, the Buddha-ship has already been wrecked; the mountain of wisdom has already collapsed."
Those who uphold the Dharma likewise desire to attain parinirvāṇa, transcending this world. Kūṭadanta,
lest wicked people engage in strife and contention,
how may the true Dharma be heard in this world so that one may find tranquility therein?
It is said that when the essential is extracted, what remains is non-essential;
apart from the light of the Tathāgata, the world no longer possesses any majestic spiritual radiance.
"Where should we go to seek [him]? At that moment, he spoke in verse:
"The world is considered empty; There is no Buddha, nothing to delight in.
What is there to search for in Jambudvīpa? One should simply attain parinirvāṇa right here."
Thereupon, the worthy Kātyāyanīputra took his bowl and robes and gave them to Upānanda, saying,
"Present these to the assembly of noble ones and proclaim my words."
"May all the worthy ones grant their forbearance; this is the noble meaning of 'Excellent,' O Venerable One—be diligent!
After the worthy Khaṇḍadravya had finished speaking these words, he entered parinirvāṇa.
After his parinirvāṇa, fire issued forth from his body and cremated him of its own accord,
like a great heap of firewood ignited by a torch.
The cremation was thus completed.
Then, from the sky, four flowing springs descended to drench his body;
the water was clear and cool,
its color like that of crystal or lapis lazuli.
That flowing water spontaneously produced a sound and spoke in verse.
The first flowing water said:
"Though wisdom dwells within the cycle of birth and death, One should not place trust in floating clouds."
The Vajra that destroys impermanence; the King of Buddha-mountains has already collapsed.
The second stream of water says:
All things are constantly in flux; why fear the harm of diligent toil?
Relinquishing oneself without attachment, the Buddha praised the peace of parinirvāṇa as the third.
Third, Śrotapāla said:
"Thus, through non-negligence, that which is practiced brings completion to one's person."
Countless afflictions and harms disturb him, like a lit lamp quickly extinguished.
The fourth stream-enterer said:
"He is the most supreme among the multitude; one should prostrate before him in reverence."
The Venerable Kāla-bhadra, having reached the bliss of parinirvāṇa,
followed the Buddha’s ten powers; may he now enter extinction like a six-tusked elephant whose calf yearns to follow its mother.
I prostrate in homage before that assembly of all worthy and noble ones;
may the venerable Sangha of the Honored Ones forgive my transgressions.
Thus, after the parinirvāṇa of the worthy Kiao-huan-po (Kauṇḍinya).
The worthy one did not take his robes and bowl by force;
in the time it takes to snap one's fingers, he immediately returned,
presented them to the assembly of monks, and completed his prostrations in due order.
Then he spoke in verse:
"The Most Honored among Men, Greatly Compassionate and Tranquil—
Upon hearing Koṇāgamana, He entered Parinirvāṇa at that very moment."
I prostrate before that assembly of all worthy and noble ones;
I pray only that the Honored Sangha will forgive my transgressions.
Having spoken thus, he then entered parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the entire assembly of monks all contemplated impermanence as being momentary,
reflecting upon the interpretations of the true sutras, the precepts, and all dharmas.
They all immediately went to the assembly of bhikṣus.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa said to Aniruddha,
"Virtuous one, please observe this assembly."
"Whoever has not yet untied the fetters of lust, anger, and delusion, nor removed the veil of craving,
must study the precepts and discern the assembly of ordinary persons.
At that time, Aniruddha, having observed those seated, addressed Mahākāśyapa.
There is a bhikṣu named Ānanda, the World-Honored One’s attendant, who is currently completing his training; he shall come to join this assembly.
Thereupon, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa—
"Venerable Ānanda, you should rise and depart.
We shall not enter into a formal agreement on the essential points of the scriptures with you."
Ānanda replied, "May the Venerable Mahākāśyapa be pleased with me; may I be without deficiency in the precepts,
free from false views, and not have corrupted my karma."
"Furthermore, he has neither lost his practice nor violated the community.
Kāśyapa replied, "Indeed,
Ānanda, you have attended upon and drawn near to the Tathāgata."
It is not at all surprising that the Most Honored One has no deficiency in his precepts.
Furthermore, you, O Benevolent One, have said:
"I have committed no transgression."

As soon as Mahākāśyapa gave rise to this thought, [Śāriputra] said: "Venerable One, do not harbor such thoughts toward me. He then spoke a verse: "If one does not know the mind of another, how can one measure their faults? I am like a person who, having dug a well, finds water and rejoices; I have attained the fruit and am likewise joyful. At that time, Mahākāśyapa felt remorse and apologized to Śāriputra. Śāriputra replied: "Venerable One, do not feel remorse. Why? Because all dharmas are empty and devoid of self-nature; they are neither born nor extinguished, and there is no transgression to be found therein. Mahākāśyapa then asked: "How is it that you have attained the fruit? Śāriputra replied: "I have attained the fruit through the non-attainment of any dharma. Mahākāśyapa said: "Excellent! Excellent! The three-thousandfold world system shook in six ways.
Hundreds of thousands of devas and humans dwelling in the void raised their voices and cried out:
"Alas! This Mahākāśyapa!"
"Why do you speak with such words?
Then the Venerable Kāśyapa said to Ānanda, "Virtuous one,
how can you say that there has been no transgression?"
"Why did you request of the Buddha that women be permitted to go forth as śramaṇīs?
Ānanda replied, "It was Mahākāśyapa, O Great One."
When the World-Honored One’s mother passed away,
Mahāmāyā Gautamī had nurtured him with great toil and personally attended to the World-Honored One.
When he was a bodhisattva, [the Buddha] nourished him with milk and raised him to maturity;
desiring to repay that kindness, he sought to have him become a śramaṇa,
out of compassion for his kinsmen and wishing to enable them to attain deliverance.
For this reason, I seek the Buddha to become a śramaṇa.
Furthermore, I have heard that the past Buddhas, upon attaining equal enlightenment, had fourfold assemblies of followers.
I reflect that the transformation through the Dharma-teachings of the World-Honored One shall not suffer any diminution.
He requested the Buddha to allow him to become a śramaṇa.
The Venerable Kāśyapa said,
"Only Ānanda is insufficient in fulfilling filial piety and repaying kindness."
Regarding the merit of making offerings to the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body,
causing women to become śramaṇas is like bringing a field of rice to full maturity.
Just as heavy rain falls and hailstones destroy [the crops], so too shall it be.
The Buddha’s True Dharma was originally destined to endure for a long time;
however, because women sat [to receive ordination] and became śramaṇas, it will remain for only a thousand years.
Furthermore, Ānanda, your statement that you sought to become a śramaṇa out of compassion for your kinsmen is inconsistent with the dharma of a śramaṇa,
because it is rooted in the affectionate concern for one's kin.
Furthermore, Ānanda, as for your statement that because there were the fourfold assembly among the Perfectly Enlightened Ones of the past,
those seeking to become śramaṇas existed at that time— [you should know that] at that time,
the worldly people’s lust, anger, and delusion were thin, and they were free from fetters and bonds.
Their aspirations were for seclusion and their minds were free from defilement;
how could they be compared to people of the present day?
This is the first fault.
He cast down his counting-sticks upon the ground.
Furthermore, Ānanda, you have another fault.
Moreover, it was said by the Blessed One:
Those who possess diligence and have attained the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) are able to dwell at will for a kalpa or even beyond a kalpa.
Why do you not seek the World-Honored One’s compassion for the sake of the world?
Ānanda replied, "Indeed, Venerable Sir.
It was because Māra Pāpīyān was agitating my mind that I did not seek mercy from the Buddha."
Kāśyapa replied: "This would be a great transgression.
What is meant by serving one who is free from desire, such that one should subdue the power of Māra, yet instead follows the teachings of Māra?"
These are the two faults.
Ānanda, you do not yet recognize these faults;
furthermore, you have another fault as well.
When the World-Honored One rebuked you, you spoke resentfully, blaming others;
by committing this offense, you incur three transgressions.
Furthermore, there is yet another transgression.
"You have stepped upon the World-Honored One’s robe woven with golden thread with your foot;
this constitutes the fourth transgression.
Ānanda, there is yet another transgression."
When the World-Honored One was about to enter parinirvāṇa,
he wished to go to the twin trees and asked you for water, but you did not give it to him.
This constitutes the fifth fault.
Furthermore, you have committed another fault:
when the Buddha, the World-Honored One, taught the various minor precepts and rules of conduct,
you did not consider to explain them for the sake of future generations when they might inquire about them.
These are the six faults.
That you displayed the World-Honored One’s private organ, concealed like that of a horse, to the multitude—
this is the seventh fault.
Ānanda, you have further faults.
Why is this? Because the World-Honored One has displayed his purple-golden complexion to women.
This caused her to weep aloud, her tears staining his feet.
These constitute the eight faults.
Ānanda, you too have committed a fault.
"In this assembly, there is no lust, anger, or delusion;
yet you alone possess the blemish of these three defilements.
You must now train yourself to accomplish the Way."
"The transformation of the assembly has been accomplished, yet you have not realized it;
this is the ninth fault.
Now, arise and leave the assembly."
"In the end, I shall never again join with you in reciting the sutras.
The worthy Ānanda surveyed the fourfold assembly;
overcome with grief, he cried out, "Alas! How bitter this is! For what reason has it come to such a pass?"
Today my body has already been separated from the Tathāgata, who provides no rescue and offers no protection;
my eyes no longer behold the Light, and the world has become dark.
Furthermore, O Venerable Mahākāśyapa:
When that Buddha, the World-Honored One, was about to pass into parinirvāṇa, he addressed Ānanda:
"Do not weep or grieve, nor burden me with this;
Mahākāśyapa has committed a minor error just now, yet you have failed to grant him forgiveness."
"O Benevolent One, Kāśyapa, you have attained joy and understanding; henceforth, you shall not lose it.
Then the Venerable Kāśyapa said to Ānanda, "Do not weep;
O Benevolent One, the roots of your merit are fully perfected."
"We shall certainly act according to these essential teachings of the Dharma.
We cannot help but offer words of direct admonition.
Ānanda, rise! I shall no longer join with you in compiling the essential scriptures."
Thereupon, the Venerable Aniruddha said to Mahākāśyapa,
"How can we part from Ānanda, who is the Buddha’s attendant?"
"Of vast learning and total retention, you are a treasury that accumulates the essentials.
You are next to the Buddha in the third rank; shall we now conclude the essentials of this sutra?
Thus spoke the Venerable Mahākāśyapa.
"We shall not join with those like Ānanda, who are still in the stage of training,
to collectively compile the meaning of the sūtras and the essentials of the Dharma. Ānanda, rise up and withdraw!"
"I and those who have attained arhatship shall together compile the scriptures.
Thereupon, Ānanda rose from his seat in sorrow;
looking back at the assembly of bhikṣus with a look of grief, he departed.
At that time, during the night, that son of the Kṛtaka clan was shown the understanding through hearing that severs all fetters;
he attained the path of Arhatship, reached the fruit of the three types of supernormal knowledge, and acquired great supernatural powers.
On another day, the assembly of arhats gathered together in numbers reaching hundreds of thousands;
like asura demons casting off the light of the moon,
their radiance shone forth, manifesting everywhere throughout the world.
Ānanda’s heart was gladdened; he was liberated from all defilements, and what was to be done had been accomplished.
Venerable Kāśyapa said, "Excellent, excellent!"
"Ānanda, since you have attained equanimity, my heart rejoices.
That which the World-Honored One called 'the accumulated teaching' has now brought you across.
Thus, following this sequence, you shall attain the severance of all outflows."

Furthermore, Ānanda, you have received the grace of that Buddha, the World-Honored One, who preached the Dharma-eye; through your extensive learning and upholding of the Dharma, it shall be established forever from this day forth.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
That Buddha dwells in the world as the most honored one; wherever he goes, he is foremost.
All there possess the people [of virtue], and their arts and practices are not uniform as they roam within this flavor of ambrosia, becoming those who have reached the stage of Samantabhadra.
The Buddha has entered the extinction of meditative concentration and is profoundly still;
for this reason, his teaching and transformation are rare. Thereupon, the elders said to Ānanda:
"You must remain and compile the authentic sūtras, the Vinaya, and the commentaries on the various dharmas."
Thereupon, the assembly, numbering hundreds of thousands, having addressed Ānanda,
contemplated the Dharma with complete reverence, profound and vast;
they universally observed the bhikṣus as they reflected upon the Buddha’s merits, which were beyond measure.
Then he spoke in verse:
"This assembly of bhikṣus is now supreme; Because they have distanced themselves from the Buddha’s virtues, They no longer possess majestic splendor, Like the sky bereft of the sun's light."
Thereupon, the venerable Ānanda beheld the lion throne,
surrounded on all sides by the assembly of bhikṣus,
like a lion king dwelling among a pride of lions.
After Ānanda had sat down, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa addressed him in verse, saying:
"O one of great wisdom, please speak! O son of the Well-Gone One, pray discourse upon it."
"What is this sutra scroll? The World-Honored One first spoke it.
As soon as Kāśyapa had finished reciting these verses for Ānanda, Ānanda’s mind immediately attained the Buddha’s awakening, and he recollected the path of the scriptures.
Free from fear and unshakable, without any doubt or hesitation,
he turned toward the place where the World-Honored One had entered parinirvāṇa;
with single-minded devotion and palms joined, he then recited this verse:
Thus have I heard at one time: the Buddha was staying at the Deer Park in Vārāṇasī, where he preached the Sūtra on the Perfect Wheel of Dharma;
a great multitude of honored ones were all present, providing mutual encouragement and assistance.
Then, ascending the lion throne, he spoke the first discourse on the "Lion's Gait," saying:
"Thus have I heard: at one time, wherever the Honored One was staying, all the sūtras that could be heard there were recited and proclaimed."
When the entire assembly of arhats heard these words, they all immediately vacated their seats and prostrated themselves upon the ground, thinking in their hearts:
"Alas! Such is the power of impermanence!"
"We ourselves have just now heard the Tathāgata preaching the Dharma;
how is it that today we hear such a thing?
At that time, the True Man spoke these verses:
Alas! The three realms are but a fleeting illusion, Like the moon reflected in water, Or like a magical conjuration, Or like a plantain tree—lacking any solidity.
The three realms have no equal; Their merit is most pure.
"The Buddha is eternally present, yet suddenly he has departed like a rising wind.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa,
after a brief moment of meditative reflection, sighed and said:
Alas! Ultimately, all efforts are without liberation.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"One who disregards the ignorant, And likewise does not protect the wise..."
Whether already liberated or not yet crossed over, there is none who does not return to extinction.
It is not by means of incantations that one is saved; it is not by avoiding coarse speech that one escapes death in this world.
All are alike, like the saltiness of the ocean waters.
Thereupon, Mahākāśyapa,
having heard these words from Ānanda,
reverently accepted the *Dharmacakrapravartana-sūtra*.
He addressed the five bhikṣus, including Ājñātakauṇḍinya:
"Is what you have received like this or not? They replied: "It is so, it is so."
They compiled the collection of the Sūtra-piṭaka by way of analogy;
they compiled the Vinaya-piṭaka and the Abhidharma-piṭaka.
At the time of compiling the Sūtras:
The devas immediately came and stood in the sky, raising their voices and proclaiming:
"O Supreme among the Multitudes, Ānanda! You who manifest all teachings and prohibitions and have compiled this Sūtra of the True Dharma, we take pity upon the multitude of people."
Thereupon, having gathered the practice with precision, Śākyamuni, the skillful guide,
for the sake of those in the future and the present, attained the foremost concentration;
he then compiled the true Sūtras and Vinaya, and having mastered all dharmas, he established the prohibitions.
The Venerable Mahākāśyapa then spoke in verse:
"This is for the sake of compassion for humanity; The Dharma-sūtra thus established is the compilation of the teachings of the One of Ten Powers, Which are indeed immeasurable."
Regarding those worldly wrong views and the recollection of the profound darkness that extinguishes their light,
Kāśyapa, kindle the great lamp within the gloom; this is from the *Kāśyapa-saṃyukta Sūtra*.
